prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: Across all five frames, the bright lower region places the camera wearer's torso and hands roughly 0.2–0.6 m away, while the darker ground and vegetation extend about 1–3 m in front; the hose-like curved object crosses the near-to-middle field at approximately 0.4–1.2 m. Other people are only partly visible near the upper edges, generally about 1–2 m from the wearer and farther away than the wearer's body, with one person toward the upper left in frame 1, legs near the upper middle in frames 2–3, and people toward the upper right in frames 4–5. The sequence suggests modest camera turning rather than a clear approach or retreat: the near torso stays at a similar distance while the people and background shift laterally. Depth makes the foreground/background ordering and approximate reach zone clearer than RGB, but it is unreliable at silhouettes, on the thin hose, and near the overexposed right side; it also merges some people and background regions into similar dark depths.
descriptions.segmentation: The masks consistently isolate the large foreground person region corresponding to the camera wearer's torso and arms, showing that these surfaces occupy most of the lower centre and are within roughly 0.2–0.7 m, while partial people appear near the upper or side boundaries about 1–2 m away. In frame 1, overlapping person-coloured masks at lower left/centre help expose occlusion boundaries, but the large green region labelled elephant is actually aligned with the wearer's foreground body in the RGB and is therefore an unreliable class assignment; the bird label in frame 3 is likewise unsupported spatially. Across frames 2–3 the foreground body remains central while a partly visible person's legs sit above it, and in frames 4–5 the person masks move toward the upper-right/right edge as the viewpoint turns. Segmentation makes occupied image area, overlap, and partial out-of-frame bodies clearer than RGB, but it misses the hose and many limbs, merges adjacent body regions, and cannot by itself determine facing direction, gaze, or metric distance reliably.
descriptions.pose: The magenta traces mainly localize visible hands: one hand cluster lies near the upper-left/centre in frame 1, paired hand shapes appear left of centre in frames 2–3, and a hand pair shifts to the upper-right in frames 4–5; these hands are approximately 0.3–0.8 m from the camera and generally within the camera wearer's arm's reach. Yellow body keypoints appear chiefly in frames 2–3, extending from the hand/upper-body area toward the lower-right or downward, but they are sparse and do not form a reliable full-body orientation; no dependable head or eye keypoints establish whether another person faces or looks toward the wearer. The lateral shift of the hand skeletons supports a turning viewpoint, while their broadly similar size gives little evidence of substantial approach or retreat. Pose makes small articulated hand locations and some limb connections easier to see than RGB, but it misses most partially cropped people, confuses or fragments joints under occlusion, and provides no stable skeleton for estimating distances between people.
